questions.q: What is the centromere index (CI) of a human chromosome whose short arm measures 2.1 µm and long arm measures 5.9 µm, and what morphology class does it belong to?
questions.a: CI = (2.1 / (2.1 + 5.9)) × 100 = 26.25% → submetacentric (CI 25–37). A wrong answer of "metacentric" reveals the student used absolute arm length difference instead of the ratio; a wrong answer of "acrocentric" reveals confusion between CI threshold for submetacentric (25%) and acrocentric (<25%).

questions.q: Explain why telomeres shorten with each round of DNA replication in somatic cells but not in germ cells, and name the enzyme responsible for this difference.
questions.a: DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the 5′ end of the lagging strand (end-replication problem), causing progressive telomere shortening in somatic cells; germ cells express telomerase (a reverse transcriptase with an RNA template) that adds TTAGGG repeats, maintaining length. A wrong answer citing "DNA ligase" or "helicase" reveals the student confuses replication machinery with the specialised telomere-maintenance enzyme.

questions.q: A metaphase chromosome shows a centromere so close to one end that the short arm appears as a mere stalk with a satellite. The total chromosome length is 6.0 µm and the short arm (including stalk) is 0.9 µm. Calculate the centromere index and state the chromosome type and its human karyotype group.
questions.a: CI = (0.9 / 6.0) × 100 = 15% → acrocentric (CI < 25%). Human acrocentric chromosomes are 13, 14, 15, 21, 22, Y → Group G. A wrong CI of 15% but classification as "telocentric" reveals the student does not know humans lack true telocentric chromosomes; a wrong group assignment (e.g., Group E) reveals confusion between acrocentric and submetacentric groups.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the functional roles of centromere and telomere during mitosis. Why would a chromosome lacking a functional centromere fail to segregate, while a chromosome lacking functional telomeres would fuse end-to-end?
questions.a: Centromere: nucleates kinetochore → microtubule attachment → segregation. Telomere: forms T-loop/shelterin complex → hides DNA end from NHEJ repair machinery → prevents fusion. No centromere = no kinetochore = random segregation/loss. No telomere = exposed double-strand break recognised by DNA-PK/Ku70/80 → ligation to another broken end → dicentric chromosome → breakage-fusion-bridge cycles. A wrong answer swapping the roles reveals the student memorised definitions but not mechanistic consequences.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Centromere position is the sole determinant of chromosome morphology in a standard karyotype." Support your evaluation with two pieces of evidence from human cytogenetics.
questions.a: The statement is FALSE. Evidence 1: Banding patterns (G/Q/R) reveal internal structure (euchromatin/heterochromatin distribution) independent of centromere position — two submetacentric chromosomes (e.g., chr 4 vs chr 5) differ in banding despite similar CI. Evidence 2: Secondary constrictions (nucleolar organiser regions on acrocentric chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, 22) create visible satellites/stalks that modify apparent morphology without changing centromere index. A student calling the statement "true" reveals over-reliance on CI alone and ignorance of banding/secondary constriction landmarks used in clinical karyotyping.

questions.q: Design a hypothetical human chromosome that would be classified as metacentric by centromere index but would likely be misidentified as submetacentric on a routine G-banded karyotype. Justify your design with specific banding pattern features.
questions.a: Design: Total length 8 µm, p-arm 4 µm, q-arm 4 µm (CI = 50% → metacentric). Insert a large heterochromatic block (C-band positive, G-band dark) spanning 3 µm of the q-arm near the centromere, while the p-arm remains entirely euchromatic (G-band light). On G-banding, the dense dark region on q makes it appear "shorter" visually, mimicking a submetacentric CI ~35%. Justification: G-banding stains AT-rich heterochromatin dark; visual arm-length estimation by eye (common in rapid screening) is biased by staining intensity, not physical length. A poor answer lacking specific banding terminology (C-band, G-band, heterochromatin) reveals the student cannot integrate cytogenetic staining principles with morphology classification.
